reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard rheumatology references
clinicalPearls: A systemic autoinflammatory disorder characterised by the classic triad of high spiking (quotidian) fevers, arthritis, and an evanescent salmon-coloured rash
The rash is typically transient, appearing with fever spikes and fading between them, often over the trunk and proximal limbs
Sore throat is a frequently reported early symptom
Strikingly high serum ferritin with a low glycosylated (fraction) ferritin is a supportive laboratory clue
Neutrophilic leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, and deranged liver enzymes are common
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful exclusion of infection, malignancy (especially lymphoma), and other autoimmune disease
IL-1 and IL-6 directed biologic therapies are effective in refractory disease, reflecting the central role of these cytokines
Macrophage activation syndrome is a life-threatening complication that must be recognised promptly
reference.pathophysiology: Adult-onset Still disease is driven by innate immune activation with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines, notably interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6, and interleukin-18, producing systemic inflammation affecting joints, skin, reticuloendothelial system, and serosal surfaces. Uncontrolled activation of macrophages and cytotoxic lymphocytes can precipitate a cytokine-storm state (macrophage activation syndrome / secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis).
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis and other systemic infections (including viral and endocarditis)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases
Reactive arthritis or other inflammatory arthritides
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin (including glycosylated fraction) and acute-phase reactants
Full blood count, liver function tests, and blood film
Extensive infection screen and blood cultures to exclude sepsis
Autoantibodies (ANA, rheumatoid factor) which are characteristically negative
Imaging and, where indicated, lymph node or bone marrow biopsy to exclude malignancy and assess for haemophagocytosis
redFlags: Features of macrophage activation syndrome: rapidly rising ferritin, falling cell counts, coagulopathy, hepatic dysfunction, and clinical deterioration
Persistent lymphadenopathy or atypical features raising concern for lymphoma
Haemodynamic instability suggesting sepsis or a cytokine-storm state
Cardiorespiratory involvement such as myocarditis, pericardial tamponade, or pleuritis
reference.prognosis: Course is variable, ranging from a self-limited monocyclic illness to a relapsing systemic pattern or a chronic destructive arthritis; overall outcomes are good with modern immunomodulatory and biologic therapy, though macrophage activation syndrome carries significant mortality if not treated urgently.
pitfalls: Labelling the illness as Still disease before adequately excluding infection and malignancy
Overlooking evolving macrophage activation syndrome amid apparently worsening disease
Attributing the transient rash to a drug reaction
Missing the significance of markedly elevated ferritin
management: NSAIDs for symptom control in mild disease and initial management
Systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay for active systemic and severe disease
Steroid-sparing DMARD therapy, principally methotrexate, for chronic and articular disease
Biologic therapy targeting IL-1 (anakinra, canakinumab) or IL-6 (tocilizumab) for refractory or corticosteroid-dependent disease
Urgent recognition and aggressive treatment of macrophage activation syndrome with high-dose corticosteroids, anakinra and ciclosporin
Exclude infection and malignancy, especially lymphoma, before and during immunomodulatory treatment
Rheumatology-led monitoring of disease activity, ferritin and organ involvement
